meta.name: VesselWatch flight medicine playbook
meta.scope: Decision support for astronaut circulation, heart and wellbeing self-checks on long missions. Not a diagnostic device.
policy: No drug doses. Treatment rules point to the protocol, not milligrams.
Every rule names its evidence level. Demo thresholds must be replaced by clinician-set values before real use.
The crew medical officer sees only what they need to act. Mood and sleep stay private unless the crew member chooses to share.
severityMeaning: Needs a closer look. The medical officer is told what to do, nothing more.
Act now. The medical officer and Earth are told.

evidenceLevels.nasa-protocol: Published NASA standard or technical brief
evidenceLevels.clinical-red-flag: Standard emergency warning sign in clinical practice
evidenceLevels.peer-reviewed: Peer-reviewed study, not a NASA operational rule
evidenceLevels.demo-threshold: Placeholder threshold chosen for the demo; needs a clinician's value

sources.MTB007: NASA OCHMO-MTB-007, Venous Thrombosis in Spaceflight, Jan 2026
sources.STD100: NASA OCHMO-STD-100.1A, requirement 6041: jugular screening L-12/3 m, L+30 d, L+60 d, R-42 d, as clinically indicated
sources.MG2019: Marshall-Goebel et al., JAMA Network Open 2019: 6 of 11 ISS crew with stagnant or retrograde jugular flow, 1 clot
sources.AC2020: Aunon-Chancellor et al., NEJM 2020: first in-flight jugular clot, treated on orbit
sources.MTB001: NASA OCHMO-MTB-001, Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome
sources.GH2000: Ghiadoni et al., Circulation 2000: brief mental stress reduced artery dilation for up to about 4 hours
sources.MIL2005: Miller et al., University of Maryland 2005-2011: laughter and joyful music increased artery dilation in small studies
sources.MIR: Barratt and Hamilton, cited in Grenon et al. 2005: arrhythmias were the second most common medical issue on Mir
sources.MIR1997: Mir 1997 Progress collision; NASA human factors analysis lists fatigue as a contributing factor
sources.MARS500: Basner et al., PNAS 2013: gradual, individual decline in activity and sleep over 520 days
sources.TR2022: Trudel et al., Nature Medicine 2022: about 54% more red blood cells destroyed in space
sources.SPRINT: NASA SPRINT study: shorter, higher-intensity exercise maintained fitness in flight
sources.CVRISK: NASA HRP Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes
sources.OSD575: NASA OSDR OSD-575, SpaceX Inspiration4 blood serum data: comprehensive metabolic panel, cardiovascular serum biomarkers and cytokine panels, 4 civilian crew, pre-flight and post-flight draws
sources.ISSEX: ISS crews schedule about 2 hours of exercise a day (resistive, treadmill and bike), per NASA exercise guidance

datasets.contents: Comprehensive metabolic panel; cardiovascular serum biomarker panel; immune and inflammatory cytokine panels
datasets.timepoints: Pre-flight L-92, L-44, L-3; post-flight R+1, R+45, R+82, R+194 (as summarized by a third-party repository; confirm on the OSDR page)
datasets.howUsed: Shows the design the agent follows: several pre-flight draws give each person their own baseline, and later draws are compared against it. The data is not used to set thresholds.

signals.baselineSleepH: This person's usual sleep in hours
signals.shortNights: Consecutive nights more than 1 h under baseline
signals.symptoms: List of: headache, puffy, neck, palp, vision, chest, breath, severeHead, neuro, exertionFatigue
signals.scan.day: Flight day of the last jugular ultrasound
signals.risk.family: Unprovoked clot in an immediate family member (true/false)
signals.exerciseMin7d: Average exercise minutes per day over the last 7 days
signals.baselineHR: This person's usual resting heart rate (bpm)
signals.hrHighDays: Consecutive days with resting HR 10+ bpm over baseline
signals.anticoagCoverageDays: Days of anticoagulant on board for this crew member
signals.anticoagCourseDays: Days still needed to finish the planned course
signals.labsOutOfRange: Lab markers outside this person's own pre-flight range at a scheduled blood draw (list of marker names)
signals.fired: Set by planDay(): ids of rules that matched today, usable in maintenance conditions

rules.title: Chest pain or sudden breathlessness
rules.why: Could mean a clot has travelled to the lungs, or a heart problem. These never wait for the next check-in.

actions.text: Stop what you're doing and stay still
Medical officer comes to you now: vitals, oxygen level, heart tracing
Emergency call with Earth flight surgeons

rules.say: This needs your medical officer right now. Stop what you're doing and stay where you are. Your medical officer is on the way, and Earth is being called.

rules.title: Sudden severe headache, vision loss, weakness or slurred speech
rules.why: Signs of a possible brain emergency, including a clot in the brain's own veins. Time matters.

actions.text: Medical officer runs a quick neuro check with you now
Emergency call with Earth flight surgeons
Hold all critical tasks

rules.say: These signs need checking right now. Stay where you are. Your medical officer is coming, and Earth is being called.

rules.title: Suspected clot on the neck scan
rules.why: NASA's protocol starts treatment as soon as a clot is seen, symptoms or not. The first ISS case had no symptoms at all.

actions.text: Start NASA clot treatment protocol with the medical officer
No spacewalks or resistive exercise for at least 30 days
Images and plan to Earth flight surgeons, priority
Check anticoagulant stock covers the full course

rules.say: Your scan shows a possible clot in a neck vein. You're stable, and there is a clear plan for this. Your medical officer will start the treatment protocol with you, and your spacewalk is on hold.

rules.title: Anticoagulant stock won't cover the course
rules.why: In the 2019 ISS case, therapy depended on a cargo ship bringing more medicine. On a Mars transit there is no resupply.

actions.text: Flight surgeon plans coverage for the full course
Recount stock and log it

rules.say: Your medicine supply is shorter than your planned course, so your flight surgeon is planning how to cover it.

rules.title: On an anticoagulant with landing in 2 days or less
rules.why: NASA recommends pausing anticoagulants before landing in case of injury: 48 hours for treatment, 24 hours for prevention.

actions.text: Plan the pre-landing pause with the flight surgeon
Confirm timing with the crew member

rules.say: Landing is close, so your medical officer will confirm when to pause your medicine, as NASA recommends.

rules.title: Head, face or neck symptoms, no scan today
rules.why: NASA weighs headache, neck swelling and facial puffiness beyond normal adaptation as possible signs of altered neck-vein flow. A scan answers it; guessing doesn't.

actions.text: Neck ultrasound within 24 hours

rules.say: In space, a headache or a puffier face can come from how blood moves in your neck, and you wouldn't feel that. So I've asked your medical officer for a quick scan today. Nothing else changes.

rules.title: Stagnant flow plus a personal risk factor
rules.why: NASA pairs stagnant flow with family history, thrombophilia or higher-risk hormones for preventive treatment.

actions.text: Flight surgeon reviews preventive protocol
Scan more often

rules.say: Your last scan showed slow blood flow in a neck vein, and your records show a risk factor. Your flight surgeon is reviewing a preventive plan.

rules.title: Stagnant flow, no risk factors
rules.why: Per NASA, this means closer watching and hydration, not medication.

actions.text: More frequent neck scans
Hydration goal added to your day
Ask Earth about fluid-shift countermeasures such as lower body negative pressure or thigh cuffs

rules.say: Your last scan showed slow flow in a neck vein. No medicine needed. We'll scan more often, and I'll remind you to drink more water.

rules.title: Heart racing or skipping
rules.why: Rhythm problems were the second most common medical issue on Mir, and several were silent. A recording settles it.

actions.text: Medical officer reviews 24 h wearable heart recording

rules.say: I've asked your medical officer to look at your heart recording from the last day. If it gets worse, or you feel faint, tell me straight away.

rules.title: Resting heart rate above your usual for 3 days
rules.why: A steady rise can come from dehydration, deconditioning, poor sleep, stress or infection. Worth a look before it becomes a problem.

actions.text: Medical officer reviews trend, hydration and sleep

rules.say: Your resting heart rate has been higher than usual for a few days. I've asked your medical officer to take a look.

rules.title: Gradual vision change
rules.why: Most long-duration crew show some eye changes (SANS), usually without other symptoms. It's checked with eye exams.

actions.text: Eye exam and vision self-test this week

rules.say: Vision changes are common on long missions. I've booked an eye check with your medical officer this week.

rules.title: Spacewalk within 3 days while not at baseline
rules.why: Fatigue came before the 1997 Mir collision. Critical tasks get a go or no-go check when someone isn't at their baseline.

actions.text: Go or no-go review with commander and medical officer

rules.say: Your spacewalk is close, so the commander and your medical officer will do a quick go or no-go check with you.

rules.title: Lab marker outside your own pre-flight range
rules.why: Blood markers vary a lot between people, so each result is compared with that person's own pre-flight draws, the design used in the Inspiration4 blood studies. One result out of range is a reason to look, not a diagnosis.

actions.text: Flight surgeon reviews the result against your pre-flight baseline
Repeat the draw if the flight surgeon asks

rules.say: One of your blood results is outside your own usual range. Your flight surgeon will compare it with your pre-flight tests. One result on its own isn't a diagnosis.

rules.title: Landing within 7 days
rules.why: Back in gravity, blood pools in the legs and people can feel faint on standing. Fluid loading and compression garments help, and on Mars there is no recovery team.

actions.text: Landing checklist: fluid loading plan and compression garment fit check
Stand test before landing day

rules.say: Landing is under a week away. Let's start your landing checklist: a fluid plan and a fit check for your compression garment.

rules.title: Exercise well under plan this week
rules.why: Without daily exercise the heart and muscles decondition. Shorter, harder sessions maintained fitness in NASA's SPRINT study.

actions.text: Swap in a short high-intensity session tomorrow

rules.say: Your exercise has been light this week. Want to try a shorter, harder session tomorrow? It still counts.

rules.title: Unusual tiredness on exertion after 3+ months
rules.why: The body destroys more red blood cells in space, so anemia is possible on long missions.

actions.text: Add a blood count to the next scheduled blood draw

rules.say: Feeling more tired than usual during exercise is worth checking after months in space. I've added a blood count to your next scheduled blood test.

rules.title: Three or more rough nights or low days
rules.why: Sleep and mood slide gradually and differently for each person. Early signals come before crises, so this stays private but gets offered support.

actions.text: Pre-sleep lighting and a wind-down routine tonight
Offer a private note to the Earth psychology team

rules.say: That's a few rough nights in a row. Want me to send a private note to the support team on Earth? Only they would see it.

rules.title: One short night or a low mood today
rules.why: Brief stress and short sleep make arteries less able to relax for a few hours. Noticed early, it stays private and just shapes the day.

actions.text: Lighter start today if the schedule allows

rules.say: Rough night. That happens a lot out here. Go a bit easier this morning if you can, and tell me if anything else feels off.

fallback.title: At your baseline
fallback.why: Nothing new. Routine schedule, and a small habit for good mood.

actions.text: Routine day. Next neck scan on the standard schedule
Bank one good moment for a harder day

fallback.say: Everything looks like your usual. Nice. Want to bank one good moment for a harder day?

maintenance.note: Daily missions are generated from today's signals and the rules that matched. Goals marked demo are placeholders for a clinician or the crew's own plan.

tasks.title: Symptom check
tasks.why: Headache, puffiness or neck swelling are early signs NASA weighs for neck-vein problems. Ten seconds a day.

tasks.title: Hydration
tasks.why: Fluid shifts reduce blood volume. Steady drinking supports circulation.

tasks.title: Extra hydration
tasks.why: NASA's protocol adds hydration when neck-vein flow is stagnant.

tasks.title: Exercise block: resistive and aerobic
tasks.why: Daily exercise protects heart, vessels and muscle against deconditioning.

tasks.title: Short high-intensity session
tasks.why: Shorter, harder sessions maintained fitness in NASA's SPRINT study. It still counts.

tasks.title: Aerobic only: bike or treadmill, no resistive machine
tasks.why: With a clot, NASA restricts resistive exercise for at least 30 days. Bike and treadmill can be considered without harness shoulder straps.

tasks.title: Neck scan with your medical officer
tasks.why: Scans on flight days 30 and 60, more often with stagnant flow, and whenever symptoms suggest one.

tasks.title: Treatment check-in with your medical officer
tasks.why: Daily contact while the clot protocol runs.

tasks.title: Vision self-test
tasks.why: A weekly one-minute check catches gradual eye changes (SANS) between exams.

tasks.title: Blood draw
tasks.why: Scheduled in-flight blood tests check for anemia and other changes against your pre-flight baseline.

tasks.title: Landing checklist: fluid plan, garment fit, stand test
tasks.why: Prepares your body for gravity. On Mars there is no recovery team.

tasks.title: Bank one good moment
tasks.why: Positive moments help on harder days, and small studies link positive emotion to healthier artery function.
